title: Class 5 Maths Ways to Multiply and Divide (NCERT Ch 13 Study Guide + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Ways to Multiply and Divide Guide
meta_desc: A clear study guide to Class 5 Maths ways to multiply and divide, with smart strategies, worked shopping case studies and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 13 is less about a single method and more about choosing the smart one. Here is how breaking numbers apart, using tens and estimation play out in real shopping and planning problems, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Stand near the notebook rack in any stationery shop in July and you will hear a parent doing mental maths out loud: notebooks at ₹24 each, the school list says 125 of them, so how much is the bill? That single question is the whole of Class 5 Maths ways to multiply and divide in one breath — a big multiplication, done under pressure, with a shopkeeper watching. NCERT Chapter 13 exists to make that moment calm instead of panicky.

Here is the thing most children miss: this chapter is not asking you to learn a brand-new multiplication method. You already met the standard column method in Class 4. What Chapter 13 adds is judgement — knowing which trick fits which number so you are not grinding through a full column sum when a ten-second shortcut would do.

What NCERT Chapter 13 actually teaches

Strip away the illustrations and the chapter is built on four moves for handling larger numbers. Children who treat these as separate topics struggle; children who see them as a toolkit — pick the right one for the job — sail through.

  • Breaking numbers apart (the distributive idea): split a number by place value, multiply the parts, add them back. 32 × 14 becomes 32 × 10 plus 32 × 4.
  • Multiplying and dividing by tens: 47 × 10 just gains a zero to make 470; 720 ÷ 9 is easier once you see it as 72 tens shared by 9.
  • Estimation first: round the numbers, get a rough answer, then check your exact answer against it. If they are wildly apart, you slipped somewhere.
  • The standard column method: the reliable fallback when the numbers are awkward and no shortcut is obvious.

Choosing the smart strategy for larger numbers

In my experience tutoring Class 5, the biggest jump happens the day a child stops reaching for the column method automatically and starts asking ‘is there an easier way here?’ That question is the real syllabus. The table below is how I get them to match the number to the move.

SituationSmart moveWorked example
One number ends in zerosMultiply or divide by tens36 × 20 = 36 × 2 × 10 = 720
A tidy two-digit numberBreak it apart by place value25 × 12 = 250 + 50 = 300
You only need a ballparkEstimate by rounding39 × 21 ≈ 40 × 20 = 800
Sharing into equal groupsDivide, then check with multiply360 ÷ 12 = 30 (since 30 × 12 = 360)
Awkward numbers, no patternStandard column method367 × 48

Case study 1: the school stationery order

Back to that shop. A school orders 125 notebooks at ₹24 each. Rather than a full column sum, break the 24 apart: 125 × 24 = 125 × 20 + 125 × 4. That is 2500 + 500 = ₹3000. Clean, and you can do it standing up.

Now the division twist that Chapter 13 loves. The school actually had a budget of ₹3000 and, at the last minute, switched to gel pens costing ₹15 each. How many pens fit the budget? 3000 ÷ 15 = 200 pens. Notice the check: 200 × 15 = 3000, so the answer holds. Multiplication and division are two views of the same picture, and pairing them is how you catch mistakes.

Why estimation saves the day here

Before dividing, a quick estimate keeps you honest: ₹3000 shared at roughly ₹15 is roughly 3000 ÷ 15, and since 15 × 200 is 3000, about 200 pens feels right. If a child had scribbled 20 or 2000, the estimate would flag it instantly.

Case study 2: planning the class picnic

A picnic needs transport for the whole of Class 5. There are 8 buses and each seats 45 students. Total seats? Estimate first: 8 × 45 is close to 8 × 50 = 400, so expect a little under that. Exact: 8 × 45 = 8 × 40 + 8 × 5 = 320 + 40 = 360 seats.

At the venue the teacher wants students seated in equal rows of 12 for a group photo. Rows needed? 360 ÷ 12 = 30 rows. Same numbers, opposite operation — and the estimate (about 360 shared by 12 is around 30) confirms it. These are exactly the passage-style problems Chapter 13 sets, where you read a real situation, decide whether to multiply or divide, and defend the answer.

How to practise this chapter well

Do not drill 40 identical sums. That builds speed at one method and none of the judgement the chapter is really testing. Instead, mix the question types so the child must decide each time: is this a break-apart, a times-ten, an estimate, or a genuine column sum? A page of five varied word problems teaches more than a page of thirty look-alike ones.

One honest caveat: estimation feels pointless to many children at first — ‘why guess when I can just work it out?’ The answer only lands when an estimate catches a real error of theirs. So let them make the mistake, then show how a ten-second estimate would have saved them. That single moment does more than a lecture.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

The free eight-question quiz below covers all four moves — breaking apart, times-tens, estimation and division — at exactly Class 5 level. Work through it, read the explanations for anything missed, and when your child is ready for full passage-style practice, the case-study e-book at the end walks through solved shopping and planning problems just like the two above.

faq.q: What does NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 13 cover?
faq.a: It covers ways to multiply and divide larger numbers — breaking numbers apart by place value, multiplying and dividing by tens, estimating answers by rounding, and the standard column method — all set inside shopping and planning word problems.

faq.q: Is this the same as long multiplication and long division?
faq.a: Not quite. Those are single methods; this chapter is about choosing the smartest method for the numbers in front of you, so a quick break-apart or times-ten shortcut often beats a full column sum.

faq.q: Why does the chapter push estimation so hard?
faq.a: Because a rough answer catches big mistakes. If a child rounds 39 × 21 to 40 × 20 = 800 and then calculates 8000, the mismatch shows something went wrong before the marks are lost.

faq.q: How should my child practise this chapter?
faq.a: Mix the question types rather than repeating one. Five varied word problems that force a choice between multiplying and dividing teach far more judgement than thirty identical sums.
